name: Podoko (Parkwa)
overview: A mountain people of the Mandara Mountains, long withdrawn into itself, the Podoko (Parkwa) say they came from Gaza by way of Waza and the Logone. The mountains, their cradle and refuge, shelter their sacred places; millet and bean farming, small livestock and forging sustain them, and the Dilda and harvest festivals punctuate the year.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Homogeneous group, in the majority in its area, united with the Podoko of Oudjila and the South; neighbour of the Mouktélé.
Podoko speakers are found in Garoua, Douala and Yaoundé.
Long closed to the outside, the Podoko today readily marry outside the group.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The mountains are their cradle and refuge, hence their religious value.
Having set out from Gaza, they stayed at Waza and along the Logone, with which they keep ties.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The chief and the lawanes (3rd-degree chiefs) organise society; decisions come from the grassroots and bind the whole community.
Each follows their own lineage; one lineage inherits from another only if the latter dies out.
Trades passed from father to son and from mother to daughter: blacksmiths (hoes, knives), healers, potters (canaris and earthenware vessels).
Good relations with the neighbours; a superior is greeted with respect.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; it is the woman who joins her husband, never the reverse.
The boy becomes a man through marriage: he lives for two years in his father's compound, where his father advises him, then builds his house.
Steps: engagement, taking care of the fiancée for a year, a sum for her plates and her clothes, then request for the girl's departure.
Bride price: goats to “reopen the door” of the in-laws, deprived of their daughter; the bride price for the engagement; a mat and millet that accompany the wife in case of misfortune.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cults: tsaltiwa (“pouring water”) in case of misfortune, toulimouta (“paying honour”) at a death, daftaouda in memory of the ancestors, mbourvazvaza before the harvest to thank God when the millet is ripe.
Sacred places: Moutsdilda in front of the chief's gate, Dzaougldama on the mountain, Aroldama; all recall actions of the ancestors.
Birth ensures the continuity of the group; death takes one back to the forebears, whom one accompanies with honour and who return in dreams.
Taboos: talking about sexuality, punishing a girl. Prohibitions: incest, adultery, theft, fights, crimes.
The thief pays back double (two goats stolen, two returned and two for the chief); adultery is punished with a fine and the loss of one's fields; incest, with exile.
To decide, people meet, speak in parables and hold a ritual.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade. Women: bean growing, selling fritters, small-scale livestock rearing.
The land belongs to the village chief; it is accessed by purchase or through the neighbourhood chief.
Ancestral crafts: hoes, sickles, mortars, mats.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: gandoura, boubou, now also jeans; women: three-piece wrapper, kaba.
Traditional medicine remains widely used: effective and cheap.
Beauty: good morals, a fine bearing, tall stature, hard work, for both sexes.
Courtship: the man must have land to cultivate, offer jewellery and wrappers, dance well; the woman relies on her bearing, her morality and offers clothes and shoes.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: richiga, ritimé, rikode, mbidijé, dili mazawa, ritilegue; instruments: guitar, drum, tam-tam, flute.
Dances: mazawa at deaths, diawa at ceremonies and festivals.
Festivals: Dilda in August, pre-harvest festival in October, harvest festival in November.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Group very attached to its traditions; its cults distinguish it from the Mandara and the Kanuri.

sections.title: The names
items: The structure of names varies according to the place of birth; the name depends on the circumstances, otherwise the name of a chosen person is taken.
A person may bear two or three names to stand out from namesakes, but the original name remains.
People are addressed according to age, respect and family rank; appellatives: dama, mtsala, aba, koundrmaya, ama.
The founding ancestor, Matbaya, is “the father of the Podoko”.

lessons.title: Who are the Podoko (Parkwa)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Podoko (Parkwa) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Podoko (Parkwa) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Podoko (Parkwa) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Podoko (Parkwa) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Podoko (Parkwa) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Podoko (Parkwa) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Homogeneous group, in the majority in its area, united with the Podoko of Oudjila and of the South; neighbour of the Mouktélé. • Podoko speakers are found in Garoua, Douala and Yaoundé. • Long closed to the outside, the Podoko now readily marry outside the group. • The mountains are their cradle and refuge, hence their religious value. • Having left Gaza, they stayed at Waza and along the Logone, with which they keep ties.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A mountain people of the Mandara Mountains, long withdrawn into itself, the Podoko (Parkwa) say they came from Gaza by way of Waza and the Logone. The mountains, their cradle and refuge, shelter their sacred places; millet and bean farming, small livestock and forging sustain them, and the Dilda and harvest festivals punctuate the year.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Podoko (Parkwa) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Podoko (Parkwa)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Podoko (Parkwa) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Podoko (Parkwa) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Podoko (Parkwa)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Podoko (Parkwa), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Podoko (Parkwa).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Podoko (Parkwa), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Podoko (Parkwa).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: bean sauce, greens, millet balls, okra. • Drinks: bil-bil, dolo. • Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade. Women: bean growing, selling fritters, small livestock rearing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Podoko (Parkwa) mainly eat bean sauce, vegetables, millet balls, okra. Traditional drinks: bil-bil, dolo. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Podoko (Parkwa): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Podoko (Parkwa)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Podoko (Parkwa) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Podoko (Parkwa) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Podoko (Parkwa) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Podoko (Parkwa) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Podoko (Parkwa)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Podoko (Parkwa), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Podoko (Parkwa). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Podoko (Parkwa), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Podoko (Parkwa). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, livestock, trade. Women: bean growing, selling fritters, small livestock. • Land belongs to the village chief; access is by purchase or through the quarter head. • Ancestral crafts: hoes, sickles, mortars, mats.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Podoko (Parkwa)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Podoko (Parkwa), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Podoko (Parkwa). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Podoko (Parkwa), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Podoko (Parkwa). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rites: tsaltiwa (“pouring water”) in case of misfortune, toulimouta (“paying honour”) at a death, daftaouda in memory of the ancestors, mbourvazvaza before the harvest to thank God when the millet is ripe. • Sacred places: Moutsdilda in front of the chief's gate, Dzaougldama on the mountain, Aroldama; all recall actions of the ancestors. • Birth ensures the continuity of the group; death leads back to the ancestors, who are accompanied with honour and who return in dreams. • Taboos: talking about sexuality, punishing a girl. Prohibitions: incest, adultery, theft, fights, crimes. • The thief returns double (two goats stolen, two returned and two for the chief); adultery is punished with a fine and the loss of one's fields; incest, with exile.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cults: tsaltiwa (“pouring water”) in case of misfortune, toulimouta (“paying honour”) at a death, daftaouda in memory of the ancestors, mbourvazvaza before the harvest to thank God when the millet is ripe. Sacred places: Moutsdilda in front of the chief's gate, Dzaougldama on the mountain, Aroldama; all recall deeds of the ancestors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Podoko (Parkwa) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Podoko
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Podoko (Parkwa) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Podoko (Parkwa) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Podoko (Parkwa) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Podoko (Parkwa) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Podoko. • Greetings: Balapia, balapiaka = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Hn balapiaka = morning greeting (one person); Hn balapiakwa = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Tanga /tra, Srā, makra, Oufada, Ldma. • The founding ancestor, Matbaya, is “the father of the Podoko”. • A group very attached to its traditions; its cults set it apart from the Mandara and the Kanuri.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Podoko are the first steps towards communicating with the Podoko (Parkwa). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
